skript.thema: How Claude Opus 5's knowledge cutoff was probed with Wikipedia daily-fact quizzes

teile.name: Hook
teile.text: Your AI may be stuck in the past. Claude Opus 5 might be that houseguest.
teile.szene: Painted open-world-game poster style: black-haired man in black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses stands on a neon city street at night, puzzled, staring up at a large clock tower, medium shot, cyan glow.

teile.name: Re-hook
teile.text: How do you catch it? Wikipedia daily facts, in an 8-way multiple choice quiz.
teile.szene: Source page card highlighting the passage about the dataset of daily facts from Wikipedia and the 8-way multiple choice quiz on what happened on a given day, screenshot-style capture of the blog text.

teile.name: Error curve
teile.text: Pop quiz for robots. The error rate timeline shows roughly when it loses signal.
teile.szene: Source page card showing the passage about analyzing the error rate timeline to see roughly when a model loses signal from its training dataset, screenshot-style capture of the blog text.

teile.name: Published cutoff
teile.text: Opus 5's published reliable and overall cutoffs say May 2026. Did the quiz agree?
teile.szene: Source page card highlighting the sentence that the published reliable and overall knowledge cutoffs for Opus 5 are May 2026, screenshot-style capture of the blog passage.

teile.name: Twist
teile.text: Nope. It seems to know nothing more than January 2026, even coding package versions. Awkward.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter freezes mid-step in a dim workshop, eyebrows raised, a glowing question mark floating beside him, medium close-up, teal and amber light.

teile.name: Verdict
teile.text: Stuck in the past? Only an estimate: the quiz says January, the label says May.
teile.szene: Source page card showing the passage that Opus 5 seems to know nothing more than the previous January 2026 cutoff models, and the line that everything here is an estimate, screenshot-style capture.

teile.name: Ending
teile.text: Be sure to like, share and save this video.
teile.szene: Painted game-poster style: the cyan-glasses presenter grins on a neon street at night, a clock tower glowing behind him, medium shot, cyan and magenta light.

regeln: Within each spoken phase use multiple distinct relevant shots, roughly 3-5 seconds each for Shorts; long videos can allow purposeful longer demonstrations. Preserve continuous narration and accurate subtitle timing.
A zoom, crop, subtitle change or decorative background does not count as a new motif. Never fill missing images with candles, unrelated stock or background-only frames.
Show the main image prominently; avoid tiny repeated photos in a mostly empty vertical frame. Preserve genuine evidence and important image details.
For AI Tools Explained identify the exact tool briefly, then show genuine interface views and different source-supported examples. Never present stock or an illustration as a real tool result.
Use original urban painted open-world-game poster styling for fictional scenes and presenters; no copied game characters. Match narrated action and era.

Clear speech and readable captions alone do not make a professional video. Inspect useful motif changes and narration-image alignment over the entire video. Missing main imagery is a substantial defect.
Include mandatory spoken like, share and save calls at the correct format-specific positions. Do not replace this requirement with a different CTA.

AI Tools Explained is for viewers with a practical task. Do not read parameter counts, architecture names, pipeline tags, context lengths or benchmark claims as a substitute for useful explanation. Explain the human task, the source-supported action and a concrete limit. A generic trending-tools question failed story review twice; prefer a specific visual workflow.

The user confirmed original presenter references on 2026-10-05: Business Origin Stories uses the blue-eyed man with a fedora, grey suit, dark tie and gold pocket watch; AI Tools Explained uses the black-haired man with black leather jacket and glowing cyan glasses. Preserve identity and typical clothing, vary action and setting.

Introduce the correct presenter at the opening and bring that same presenter back during the video in useful actions. Do not confine the figure to the ending. Do not replace original channel figures with different fictional people; anonymous period workers remain clearly illustrative supporting people, never a real-founder likeness.

Prefer vivid original painted open-world-game scenes to long holds on lifeless documentary photos. Preserve factual accuracy and show authentic tool examples briefly as evidence. Camera moves alone are not new motifs or full character animation.

The user confirmed on 2026-10-05 that both new delivered videos are much better than before. Preserve the original painted world, recurring channel identity, matching main imagery, music and useful scene changes. The long-term quality target remains 10/10; the user did not give these videos a numeric score. Do not replace their actual AI scores or the existing 7/10 delivery threshold with the aspirational target.

Lead with a concrete, task-oriented hook and visual proof of the tool's result in the opening seconds, avoiding vague metaphors.
Ensure direct visual alignment between narration and imagery, replacing generic office or people scenes with specific visual references to the topic, prompt, or question being discussed.
Match each spoken segment directly with relevant tool UI screenshots, output examples, or source-verified visuals.
Focus narration on practical human workflows and real tool limits rather than raw technical specifications or context lengths.
Maintain smooth logical transitions between script concepts, avoiding abrupt topic jumps or disconnected rhetoric.
Eliminate repetitive phrasing so every sentence delivers new, unique narrative value.
Synchronize visual transitions, labels, and subtitles precisely with spoken voiceover pacing.
Back factual claims with on-screen citations and verbally flag any uncertainties.
Include mandatory like, share, and save calls-to-action at format-correct positions.
Treat audience feedback as provisional data, phrasing lessons conditionally without asserting unobserved causes.
Base quality fixes on concrete, observable improvements rather than promises of views or retention.

skript.beschreibung: A blogger quizzed Claude and GPT models on Wikipedia daily facts to estimate their knowledge cutoffs. Opus 5's published cutoff is May 2026, yet it seems to know no more than January 2026 models; all results are estimates.

belege.name: Exploring Claude/GPT Knowledge Cutoffs and Pre-Training Timelines
belege.text:
Discussed on Hacker News (157 points, 2026-08-10).
PAGE TEXT (fetched today):
Exploring Claude/GPT Knowledge Cutoffs - by Shrivu Shankar
Exploring Claude/GPT Knowledge Cutoffs & Pre-training Timelines
An analysis of what models know and what it tells us about how they were trained.
We can learn hidden facts about how frontier models were trained by “probing” them with carefully curated requests.
By scoring them on niche facts we can approximate how many parameters models like GPT-5 and Opus have, using “Incompressible Knowledge Probes”
By measuring how the models break down tokens we can reveal facts about the datasets mixtures they used to train the model (or at least the tokenizer) using “Data Mixture Inference”
By scoring them on date or self-identification related questions you can also estimate training timelines ( this post )
Everything here is an estimate. It’s possible that some speculation in this post is totally incorrect given there’s not a ton of publicly available ground truth to verify against.
The 3 main stages of model training.
As a brief primer (see Alex Wa’s blog for more), how we train massive large language models has converaged into 3 stages:
Take a massive amount of general purpose data (aka scrape the internet) and “pre-train” a massive auto-complete model on that data.
Use domain-specific “textbook quality” data to improve the base models and extend certain base capabilities like long-text understanding
Turn the base model into the “assistant” persona, honing in on its personality, reasoning ability, and tool-calling.
While increasingly more compute is spent on post-training for boosting a model’s reasoning and problem solving, one of the most expensive and data-intensive steps is generating that pre-training checkpoint (by ‘checkpoint’ think of a massive claude-super-secret-2026-11-01-base.cpkt file).
While all labs operate slightly differently, what you might see (~ page 44 ) is:
The “pre-training” team kicks off and babysits a multi-month run to get a base checkpoint. These pre-training models often, but not always, imply major versions of released models (GPT-4 → GPT-5).
While that’s happening, the “capability” and “post-training” teams will run experiments for how to improve on the most recent base model. Advancements in post-training and capabilities often manifest as minor versions of released models. These teams often also “distill” a single post-trained model into smaller variants that become model families (Fable/Opus/Sonnet/Haiku, Sol/Terra/Luna). Labs may also release post-trained models from half-baked pre-training checkpoints as soon as x% of the version N+1 checkpoint is better than the 100% baked version N checkpoint.
The model released to the public is the culmination of the most recent checkpoint with the best set of capabilities and post-training techniques applied to it.
With this in mind, I was curious how much of this process you can “see” just by probing the model over the official APIs.
To estimate the pre-training checkpoint dates, I constructed a dataset of daily-facts from Wikipedia (e.g. 2025 in the United States ) and gave every model an 8-way multiple choice quiz on what happened on a given day. Then, by analyzing the error rate timeline, you can see roughly when it loses signal from its training dataset.
View the full dataset. For GPT-5.4, you can see the fact-estimated knowledge cutoff is aligned with OpenAI’s published knowledge cutoff. It’s smooth as an artifact of the model being better able to guess near-future events as well as recent in-data events being undersampled during training. This is also why I use the midpoint rather than the start or end of the curve.
You can then plot this for all models.
View the full dataset. Estimated knowledge cutoffs and published dates. Comparing model curves side-by-side in the full viewer makes it easier to see roughly where the cutoff occurred and how steep it is.
After staring at these charts for a bit, here’s what I’m speculating:
Anthropic models Opus 4.7 onwards are all from the same training run that cuts off just around late December 2025. This is derived from how they all share a very similar effective knowledge cutoff (green). A core assumption I’m making here is that the pre-training base model completion date is highly correlated with the dataset timespan used, if that’s wrong these results could be off by some offset (e.g. it’s actually Jan 2026). It’s also interesting that Opus 4.7+ models all have a published reliable and overall knowledge cutoff that’s identical — maybe that’s due to a new post-training technique being used?
OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 family comes from their own checkpoint, separate from GPT-5.5, that finished around late February 2026. This is derived from how they have a distinct effective knowledge cutoff from previous models. You’ll notice Luna looks like it can predict the future — that’s more of an artifact of it having a high error rate all around at a “low” reasoning effort.
Opus 5 is a bit unusual. The published reliable and overall knowledge cutoffs are May 2026 and yet it seems to know nothing more than previous Jan 2026 cutoff models. I did several ablations to test whether it was an artifact of the types of probing questions I used, but not really — the cutoff applies to recall on coding package versions as well.
What if you just ask the model what today is?
View the full dataset. On the dashed diagonal a model's self-model matches its factual knowledge; below it the model thinks it is living in its own past. Recent OpenAI models are excluded since the API injects the actual date into all requests (TIL! This feature really annoys a lot of folks).
It ends up being fairly correlated with fact-based estimates. If you look closely you can see some vertical lines within a few of the families of models.
GPT-4.1 nano → GPT-4.1 mini → GPT-4.1
Opus 4.7 → Sonnet 5 → Fable/Opus 5
Interpreting this graph as X = “pre-training corpus” and Y = “post-trained behavior”, these vertical strips (X constant, Y increasing) visualize active post-training
